cards.title: Unikernels were hard. key word: were

The author says an AI agent wrote **mkfs.xfs in Rust**, matching the original output, in a few hours; he argues a smaller **attack surface** leaves attackers fewer options. cards.title: C for Rust programmers

depth.text: someone wrote a guide to the **C quirks** that catch **Rust programmers** off guard
The author walks through how C strings end with a **null byte**, **arrays become pointers** when passed to functions, and **error handling** is left to the programmer.

cards.camps: Two camps: the article urges checking malloc for a null result; one commenter says overcommit often means running out of memory won't produce one, though invalid arguments still can.

comments.text: Any tutorial for C should explain compiler warnings and other tools that help make code safer. In C, you do not rely on the language specification but on tooling. Especially for Rust programmers, this needs to be explained more explicitly. And of course, you can build abstractions using types in C. So a tutorial should also focus on that, and perhaps not start with a low-level string reversal…

There is a nuanced mistake in > If your machine runs out of memory, reversed[i] will cause a segfault upon being accessed. In order to avoid unhelpful segfaults, the program should check for a null pointer and gracefully exit if one is found If overcommit is enabled (often by default), malloc will not return null when machine runs out of memory. malloc will still return null if input argument is…

Re: arrays are pointers. One of my favorite things to show just how bare this is in C is to show array access commutativity. char c = {1,2,3}
c[1] == *(c + 1)
*(c + 1) == *(1 + c)
c[1] == 1[c]
C is wonderfully simple at times.

Some fun quirks I never learned until years after first getting into C: - zero-initialization via `= {0};` will still leave padding and any data not covered by the smallest elements of unions uninitialized, so serializing data structures zeroed via that method is unsafe - A pointer that increments any more than 1 past the end of a valid memory region (e.g. the end of a buffer) is instant…

My biggest bewilderment with C is that malloc has to store the buffer size otherwise free could not work...but nobody in decades thought to make this information accessible to the programmer! If you want to keep track of buffer bounds in C, you have to do it artisanally. Despite it's, in most implementations, stored right there next to the data and thus in L1 cache already.

depth.text: someone found **DuckDB reads data from S3** much faster, without changing the query

For a query reading one column from a 2.2 GB Parquet file, the writer’s M5 laptop took **18.8 s** with DuckDB 1.5.5 and **7.7 s** with the 2.0 alpha. A separate pool of download threads fetches row groups ahead, so workers can decode while downloads continue.
data: One 2.2 GB Parquet file, one column — DuckDB 1.5.5
One 2.2 GB Parquet file, one column — DuckDB 2.0 alpha

glossary.bot traffic: Web requests made automatically by software rather than by a person.
glossary.crawler: A program that visits web pages and gathers them so a search engine can find them.
glossary.ASN: Autonomous System Number: a number used to identify a network on the internet.
glossary.data center: A building full of computers that store information and run online services.
glossary.decentralized systems: Systems spread across separate computers or sites, so they don’t all depend on one place.
glossary.POS systems: Point-of-sale systems: the devices and software stores use to ring up purchases and take payments.
glossary.WebUSB: A browser feature that lets a website communicate directly with a connected USB device.
glossary.Material Design 3 Expressive: A visual style for app screens, with distinctive layouts, colors, and animations.
glossary.cease and desist: A formal legal demand to stop doing something.
glossary.instance: One separately run copy of a service, with its own operator and users.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.front-end: The part of a service people see and use.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.self-host: Run a service on computers you manage yourself.
glossary.TOS: Terms of Service: the rules a website sets for using it.
glossary.IANAL: I Am Not A Lawyer: a quick way to say the writer isn't a lawyer.
glossary.unikernel: A way to build an application with only the operating-system pieces it needs, instead of relying on a full general-purpose system.
glossary.attack surface: All the parts of a system that an attacker might try to break into.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.userland: The parts of an operating system that run outside its central core, including many everyday programs.
glossary.Nix overlay: A way to add or change packages and fixes in a Nix setup without changing the original package set.
glossary.ultraprocessed food: Food made with extensive industrial processing, often with ingredients added to make it convenient or appealing.
glossary.insulin: A hormone the body releases to help manage sugar in the blood.
glossary.metabolic chamber: A sealed room where researchers measure how much energy someone uses and how their body burns fuel.
glossary.fMRI: Functional magnetic resonance imaging: a scan that tracks blood-flow changes to show which parts of the brain are active.
glossary.NOVA scale: A system used to group foods by how much industrial processing they go through.
glossary.glycemic index: A measure of how quickly a food can raise blood sugar.
glossary.coding agent: An AI tool that can help write or change code, often by using other tools.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: automatic checks that run when developers change code, helping catch problems early.
glossary.I-PASS: Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness, Synthesis: a written handoff that tells the next worker what happened and what to do.
glossary.differential diagnosis: A list of possible causes to check before choosing a fix.
glossary.decomposition: Breaking a large coding task into smaller tasks that can be handled and reviewed separately.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.null byte: A zero byte C uses to mark the end of a string.
glossary.pointer: A value that tells a program where something is stored in memory.
glossary.malloc: A C function that asks for a block of memory for a program to use.
glossary.overcommit: A system setting that lets programs request more memory than is currently available.
glossary.segfault: A program crash caused by trying to access memory it shouldn't.
glossary.buffer overflow: When a program reads or writes beyond the space set aside for data.
glossary.computer vision: Software that examines pictures or video to spot and identify what's shown.
glossary.projection mapping: Putting images from a projector onto real surfaces so they line up with things in the room.
glossary.spatial computing: Using computers to place information into the physical spaces around you.
glossary.popovers: Small panels that appear over a page when you tap or click something.
glossary.GPL-3: GNU General Public License version 3: rules for sharing software and changes to it.
glossary.hard paywall: A block that keeps you from reading an article unless you pay or sign in.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
glossary.constrained decoding: Making a model choose only from answers it is allowed to give.
glossary.calibration: How well a model’s confidence matches how often its choices are actually right.
glossary.temperature scaling: A way to adjust confidence scores so they better match how often answers are right.
glossary.holdout: A set of examples kept aside to check a model on data it did not train on.
glossary.fine-tuning: Training an already-built model a bit more on examples for a particular job.
glossary.macro F1: A score across answer categories that gives each category equal weight.
glossary.zero-shot classifier: A model asked to sort things into categories without examples for that task.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.S3: An online storage service where files can be kept and read over the internet.
glossary.Parquet: A file format that stores table data grouped by columns, so tools can read the columns they need.
glossary.row group: A block of rows stored together inside a data file.
glossary.async I/O: Asynchronous input/output: fetching data while other work continues, instead of sitting idle waiting.
glossary.AI: Artificial intelligence: computer systems designed to do tasks people associate with thinking.
glossary.parameter: A setting inside an AI model that helps shape what it learns and produces.
glossary.threshold of regulation (TOR): An exemption that lets certain chemicals avoid a safety review when used at very low levels in food-contact materials.
glossary.parts per billion (ppb): A way to describe a tiny amount: one part of a substance for every billion parts of a product.
glossary.hormone disruptors: Chemicals that interfere with the body’s hormone signals.
glossary.GRAS: Generally regarded as safe: a route that has let companies decide ingredients are safe without telling the FDA, according to campaigners.
glossary.emulsifiers: Substances that help ingredients that would normally separate stay mixed together.
glossary.containment: Limiting which files, connections, or other parts of a device a program can access.
glossary.JSON: A common format for storing and sending data in a way that programs can read.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.least privilege: Giving a program only the access it needs to do its job.
glossary.WSL: Windows Subsystem for Linux: a way to use Linux tools on Windows.
glossary.Nix: A tool for describing a build's inputs so the build can be repeated.
glossary.race condition: When the order of events can cause a program to end up in the wrong state.
glossary.thread schedule: The order in which a computer lets a program's threads take turns running.
glossary.derivation: A Nix build recipe that lists the source and other inputs needed to make a program.
glossary.debug symbols: Extra information that lets a debugger connect a program's running state to its source code.
glossary.VM: Virtual machine: a computer that runs inside another computer.
glossary.deterministic: Something that gives the same result when it gets the same input.
glossary.open model: An AI model shared for others to use, though “open” can mean different things.
glossary.M&A: Mergers and acquisitions: when companies combine or one company buys another.
glossary.acquihiring: Buying a company mainly to bring its employees onto your team.
glossary.compute: The processing power computers use to run AI or other software.
glossary.diffusion model: An image-making AI that starts with visual noise and gradually turns it into a picture.
